lesson.title: The Middle Ground: Why the Median Resists Outliers
lesson.summary: The median is the middle value of an ordered quantitative data set, and because it depends only on position rather than exact size, it stays stable even when extreme values or skew would badly distort the mean.
lesson.body:
The median is the middle value of a quantitative data set once every observation has been sorted from smallest to largest. When the number of observations, n, is odd, the median is simply the single value sitting exactly in the middle. When n is even, as in most of the worked examples so far in this unit, there is no single middle value, so the median is defined as the average of the two values on either side of the middle, the n-over-2 and the n-over-2-plus-1 values in the sorted list.

What makes the median especially useful is a property called resistance: because the median only depends on the position of values in an ordered list, not on their actual numeric size, extremely large or extremely small values barely affect it. Moving the largest value in a data set from, say, 100 to 100,000 does not change the median at all, as long as it stays the largest value, since its position in the sorted order never changes. The mean, by contrast, would shift enormously under the same change, since it depends on the literal sum of the values.

Home prices demonstrate this resistance clearly. Suppose six recent home sales, in thousands of dollars, were 210, 225, 230, 240, 260, and 720, where the last sale was an unusually large estate. Sorted, the data is already in order. With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth: 230 and 240, giving 235. The mean, by comparison, is the total divided by six: 210 + 225 + 230 + 240 + 260 + 720 = 1,885, and 1,885 divided by 6 is about 314.17. The median of 235 sits close to where most of the ordinary homes actually sold, while the mean of 314.17 is pulled far above that range by the single 720 outlier, illustrating exactly why the median is described as resistant and the mean is not.

This resistance is why the median is the preferred measure of center whenever a distribution is skewed or contains outliers, situations covered throughout this unit, including the skewed-left exam scores, the skewed-right home prices, and the age example under center of distribution. News reports on "median household income" rather than "average household income" reflect exactly this reasoning: a small number of extremely high earners would inflate the mean income well above what a typical household actually earns, while the median stays anchored near the realistic middle.

The tradeoff is that the median ignores most of the actual numeric information in a data set. It does not matter to the median calculation whether the largest value is 720 or 7,200, only that it remains the largest, which means the median can sometimes understate just how extreme a data set's largest or smallest values really are, even while correctly representing the typical case.

The general guideline connecting median back to the mean is straightforward: for a roughly symmetric distribution, mean and median will be close and either can be reported, but for a skewed distribution or one with outliers, the median is the more trustworthy single number, because it describes where the typical, middle case actually falls rather than being pulled toward whichever tail happens to be longer.
